Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Vignette:
The event that undid Marcus was not a bomb. After twenty-two years dismantling improvised explosive devices in conflict zones, he had developed a quiet, almost surgical relationship with controlled danger. He knew the weight of a trigger mechanism, the precise pressure required to disarm. What he could not prepare for was a wall of water. During a routine deployment following a Category 5 hurricane, Marcus was leading a team to clear debris from a flooded residential area when the levee upstream gave way without warning. The surge came as a roar, a sound that was not a blast but carried the same obliterating force. He was swept against a collapsed garage, pinned by the current as a car door slammed into his ribs. He watched a mother and her two children being pulled from their roof, and he could not reach them. He could not move. The water was brown and loud and he screamed for help that did not come for nearly forty minutes. The family did not survive. Marcus did, but something in him had been torn loose.

In the months that followed, he returned to his job, but the world had changed. A colleague shouting across the base to get his attention would send him into a cold sweat, his heart hammering before his mind could register that there was no threat. He began to notice that his body reacted before he did—a sudden loud noise, a truck backfiring, a door slamming—and he would find himself on the ground, hands over his head, breathing in ragged gasps. He had flashbacks that came without warning: the brown water, the screaming, the weight of the current. During one such episode in the mess hall, he shoved a table aside before he realized where he was. The rage that surfaced with these memories was volcanic. He would feel a burning, wordless fury at the water, at the engineers who had built the levee, at himself. But when he tried to recall the full sequence of events, the memory seemed to stop short, like a film reel that snapped mid-scene. He knew he had been underwater at one point, but the seconds between being submerged and being pulled out were a blank space he could not enter. He pushed the memory away before he could complete it, and the incompleteness gnawed at him.

To manage the constant sense of being on alert, Marcus developed a set of habits that he did not recognize as strategies. He began to avoid anything that could be stressful. He stopped answering phone calls from his unit. He declined invitations to barbecues, to birthday parties, to his wife’s work events. If a situation felt unpredictable—a new restaurant, a change in schedule, a crowded grocery store—he simply did not go. He kept his mind occupied all the time. At home, he would have the television on while scrolling through his phone while listening to a podcast, because silence was where the water waited. He began to eat excessively, often late at night after his wife had gone to bed, consuming entire pizzas or bags of chips without tasting them, just to have something to do with his hands and his mouth. His weight climbed by thirty pounds. His wife, Amara, began to sleep in the guest room because his thrashing and shouting woke her. He told her he was fine. He told himself the same thing.

What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was a moment at work. He was inspecting a suspicious package in a suburban backyard when a child in the neighboring house slammed a screen door. The sound was sharp, sudden. Marcus dropped his tools, spun around, and drew his sidearm before he had consciously registered the noise. His team looked at him with something between concern and pity. His supervisor sent him home and told him to take leave. That night, sitting alone in his living room with three different screens running, Marcus realized he could not remember the last time he had felt safe. He was terrified of his own reflexes. He was afraid that the next time his body reacted before his mind, someone would get hurt. He wanted to stop being afraid of the world. He wanted to sit in a quiet room and not hear the water.
